title: Amoxicillin
wiki_lead:
Amoxicillin is an antibiotic medication belonging to the aminopenicillin class of the penicillin family. The drug is used to treat and prevent bacterial infections such as middle ear infection, strep throat, pneumonia, skin infections, odontogenic infections, and urinary tract infections. It is taken orally (swallowed by mouth), or less commonly by either intramuscular injection or by an IV bolus injection, which is a relatively quick intravenous injection lasting from a couple of seconds to a few minutes.
Common adverse effects include nausea and rash. It may also increase the risk of yeast infections, and when used in combination with clavulanic acid, diarrhea. It should not be used in those who are allergic to penicillin. While usable in those with kidney problems, the dose may need to be decreased. Its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding does not appear to be harmful. Amoxicillin is in the β-lactam family of antibiotics.
Amoxicillin was discovered in 1958 and came into medical use in 1972. Amoxil was approved for medical use in the United States in 1974, and in the United Kingdom in 1977. It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. It is one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics in children. Amoxicillin is available as a generic medication. In 2024, it was the 22nd most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 24 million prescriptions.

Medical uses

Amoxicillin is used in the treatment of a number of infections, including acute otitis media, streptococcal pharyngitis, pneumonia, skin infections, urinary tract infections, Salmonella infections, Lyme disease, and chlamydia infections.


Acute otitis media
Children with acute otitis media who are younger than six months of age are generally treated with amoxicillin or other antibiotics. Although most children with acute otitis media who are older than two years old do not benefit from treatment with amoxicillin or other antibiotics, such treatment may be helpful in children younger than two years old with acute otitis media that is bilateral or accompanied by ear drainage. In the past, amoxicillin was dosed three times daily when used to treat acute otitis media, which resulted in missed doses in routine ambulatory practice. There is now evidence that two-times daily dosing or once-daily dosing has similar effectiveness.


Respiratory infections
Most sinusitis infections are caused by viruses, for which amoxicillin and amoxicillin-clavulanate are ineffective, and the small benefit gained by amoxicillin may be overridden by the adverse effects.
Amoxicillin is considered the first-line empirical treatment for most cases of uncomplicated bacterial sinusitis in children and adults when culture data is unavailable. grok_lead: Amoxicillin (commonly misspelled as "amoxacillin"; alternative spelling "amoxycillin" formerly used in some regions such as Australia) is a semisynthetic beta-lactam antibiotic belonging to the aminopenicillin class, developed as a derivative of penicillin by modifying the side chain to extend its spectrum to certain gram-negative bacteria. It is one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics worldwide, approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for treating a broad range of bacterial infections in primary care settings. As a bactericidal agent, amoxicillin works by binding to penicillin-binding proteins in susceptible bacteria, thereby inhibiting cell wall synthesis and leading to bacterial lysis. First introduced in the 1970s as an analog of ampicillin, amoxicillin offers enhanced oral absorption compared to ampicillin, with activity against both gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria, such as Streptococcus species and Haemophilus influenzae. It is available in various formulations, including capsules, tablets, chewable tablets, and oral suspensions, allowing for flexible dosing in adults and children. Dosage varies depending on the type and severity of the infection, the patient's age, weight, and renal function. For adults and children weighing 40 kg or more, typical doses are 250â500 mg every 8 hours or 500â875 mg every 12 hours. For children weighing less than 40 kg, doses range from 20â45 mg/kg/day, divided and given every 8 or 12 hours. Doses are oral and should be determined by a healthcare provider. Common indications include infections of the ear, nose, throat, lower respiratory tract (e.g., pneumonia and bronchitis), skin, urinary tract, and acute bacterial sinusitis, as well as eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with other agents for peptic ulcers. Off-label uses extend to conditions like Lyme disease prophylaxis and endocarditis prevention. Amoxicillin is generally well-tolerated, with a short half-life of approximately 61 minutes and primary renal excretion, necessitating dose adjustments in patients with kidney impairment. It is classified as pregnancy category B, indicating no evidence of risk in animal studies, and is considered safe for use during pregnancy by authorities such as the Mayo Clinic, commonly used without significant risks to the fetus, and is considered safe during breastfeeding with minimal transfer to infants. However, it should be avoided in individuals with penicillin allergies, and its use can interact with oral contraceptives, potentially reducing their efficacy. Complete courses are essential to prevent resistance, and it is ineffective against viral infections like the common cold or flu. If symptoms do not improve within a few days or worsen, consultation with a healthcare provider is recommended to evaluate possible viral causes, antimicrobial resistance, or the need for alternative treatment.
